doc: What runtime discovery and environment design (src/runtime/) may be told about the outside world, as DATA. This file is where a runtime, a package manager, a service or a container feature is NAMED: nothing under src/runtime/ knows one, so a new stack is a row here and an ecosystem adapter registered beside the others, never an edit to the engine. A `requirement` is what a unit needs to run, under the id an ecosystem adapter (src/ecosystems/) reports it by; `tool` names the row of catalog/tools.json that detects it on a machine, `os` the platforms it can be met on (null: any), `container` whether a Linux dev container can provide it, `feature` the dev container feature that does, and `with` another requirement that brings it along (npm comes with node). `launchers` say how a unit's declared command is RUN, `versionFiles` which tool-version files pin a requirement, `services` which images are servers a project depends on, and `environment` what a created dev container is built from, `shells` which scripts hint at the systems a checkout is run on, and `platforms` the operating systems a component's matrix is drawn over, and `connectivity` how a check of a server the checkout needs is asked from inside a container. Immutable shipped data: an upgrade may change a row.

requirements.name: .NET (modern) for Windows
requirements.doc: A modern target that names Windows (net8.0-windows) and no target that names no platform: the same SDK as .NET, and an application only a Windows machine runs, most often a desktop UI. A Linux container does not provide it.

requirements.name: .NET Framework (classic)
requirements.doc: The classic Windows framework. It is not the modern .NET, a Linux container does not provide it, and this engine does not assume Mono can stand in for it.

requirements.name: Playwright browsers and their system libraries
requirements.doc: Browsers need system libraries a dev container does not carry. No catalog feature provides them, so a proposal names the requirement and leaves how to a person.

shells.doc: Scripts a checkout keeps where a person runs them from -- its top, and a scripts directory -- and the systems each kind is written for. A checkout whose every such script is of one family is POSSIBLY run there: evidence beside the operating-system matrix, never a requirement, because PowerShell runs elsewhere too and a file name is not a runtime.

connectivity.doc: How a connectivity check is asked from INSIDE a container: a fixed script per tool an image may already have, tried in this order until one is there. `${HOST}`, `${PORT}` and `${TIMEOUT_MS}` are WHOLE argument elements the engine replaces with the value as an element of its own -- never text inside a script, and a row that puts one inside another element is dropped. Each script prints exactly one line, `<RESOLVED|FAILED|UNKNOWN> <REACHABLE|UNREACHABLE|NOT_ATTEMPTED>`, and exits 0; it sends nothing and reads nothing a server says. Orbit installs none of these tools: with none of them in the image the answer is UNKNOWN.

argv: const [h, p, m] = process.argv.slice(-3), ms = Number(m), say = (l) => { process.stdout.write(l + "\n"); process.exit(0); }, t = setTimeout(() => say("UNKNOWN NOT_ATTEMPTED"), ms); require("dns").lookup(h, { all: true }, (e) => { clearTimeout(t); if (e) return say("FAILED NOT_ATTEMPTED"); const s = require("net").connect({ host: h, port: Number(p) }); s.setTimeout(ms); s.on("connect", () => say("RESOLVED REACHABLE")); s.on("timeout", () => say("RESOLVED UNREACHABLE")); s.on("error", () => say("RESOLVED UNREACHABLE")); });
primitives.doc: Node's own resolver, then one connection with the deadline; a lookup that never answers is UNKNOWN.
getaddrinfo, then create_connection with the deadline; a port or a deadline that is not a number is never used.

argv:
case "$2$3" in ''|*[!0-9]*) echo "UNKNOWN NOT_ATTEMPTED"; exit 0;; esac
r=UNKNOWN
if command -v getent >/dev/null 2>&1; then if getent ahosts "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; then r=RESOLVED; else echo "FAILED NOT_ATTEMPTED"; exit 0; fi; fi
t=""
if command -v timeout >/dev/null 2>&1; then t="timeout $(( ($3 + 999) / 1000 ))"; fi
if $t bash -c 'exec 3<>"/dev/tcp/$1/$2"' bash "$1" "$2" 2>/dev/null; then echo "RESOLVED REACHABLE"; else echo "$r UNREACHABLE"; fi
primitives.doc: getent when the image has it (else the name is UNKNOWN), then /dev/tcp under `timeout` when the image has it; every value a quoted positional parameter.

isolation.doc: How the containers an ISOLATED sandbox starts for itself are run (ADR 0038, 0039): argument lists as data, so the engine names no runtime. The worker IMAGE is a person's (sandbox.isolation.workerImage, pinned by digest and trusted in Orbit Control); these say only what runs in it, where the plugin, a run's inputs and its outputs are mounted, and which connectivity primitive (connectivity.primitives) the worker image answers readiness and egress probes with.
